libvirt is the management abstraction layer in the KVM virtualization stack, and virsh is the command line used to communicate with it. This article focuses on the evolution of the libvirt daemon architecture, a comprehensive classification of virsh commands, the essentials of domain XML configuration, and the command-line workflows most useful in everyday administration.

libvirt is a set of virtualization management APIs that provides a unified XML configuration interface and remote-management protocol for hypervisors such as KVM, QEMU, Xen, LXC, and VMware ESX. In the KVM stack, libvirt sits here:
Domain lifecycle management: start, stop, pause, resume, migrate
Resource abstraction: Represent CPU, memory, disks, and networking in a unified XML model
Remote management: Control hypervisors remotely over SSH, TLS, TCP, and other transports
Security isolation: Support sVirt (SELinux), AppArmor, and cgroups resource limits
One daemon handles everything: VM management, networking, storage, devices, and secrets
Advantage: simple, with one service and one socket
Drawbacks: a crash in any function affects the whole daemon; coarse-grained permissions make least-privilege access difficult
Modern modular daemons (whether they are enabled depends on the distribution and installation configuration):
Fault isolation: Separate management processes can reduce the spread of some failures; network failures still affect VM connectivity
Permission granularity: Users can be granted VM-management rights without network/storage-management rights
On-demand startup: Socket activation reduces the overhead of idle daemon processes
Independent upgrades: Each module can be restarted separately

Deployment choice: First inspect the host's actual services and sockets, then choose the architecture using the official migration procedure. The nixos-unstable libvirtd module checked for this article still uses monolithic libvirtd; a version number alone does not justify claiming that all NixOS 24.05+ systems use modular daemons. The following service commands apply only to conventional systemd distributions using that architecture. Do not mix them with monolithic sockets that remain enabled. Guest-agent shutdown also requires the agent and channel; virtio-win drivers are not an inherent prerequisite for ACPI. Pool/volume operations can also write to or delete real backend resources. pool-build formats resources on some backends, and vol-delete/upload should not be used on disks that are online. Identify the owning pool, file/block device, and every consumer. Simply downloading a volume that is being written to does not produce a consistent backup. Backend support varies with the libvirt build and packages; the pool type for NFS is netfs.
libvirt storage management has two layers: a storage pool is the storage backend, and a volume is an individual disk file within the pool.

Important: An internal snapshot stores the disk snapshot inside an image that supports it; an external snapshot switches to a new overlay file. snapshot-create reads the requested configuration from XML, while snapshot-create-as constructs it from arguments. Neither command name alone identifies the snapshot type. --disk-only means memory is not saved; it does not replace checking each disk's snapshot=external/file path and chain state. Snapshots are not independent backups. TPMs, UEFI NVRAM, VFIO, external storage, and the current software version impose limitations on snapshots, rollback, and migration.

The following illustrates a workflow with internal-snapshot support. First verify the disk format, domain features, and current snapshot support, and back up any required external state. Shutdown commands are asynchronous requests; use domstate to confirm the required state before creating, reverting, or deleting snapshots. Do not apply this workflow directly to Windows VMs with VFIO, TPMs, NVRAM, or complex external chains. Consistent online snapshots require guest quiescing/agent support and application coordination. If an operation fails, do not assume the transaction succeeded as a whole.

libvirt uses XML as the single source of truth for VM configuration. Understanding the domain XML structure is essential to mastering libvirt.

Each snippet is a separate example. The topology's sockets × dies × cores × threads must match the total vCPU count. host-model does not guarantee live-migration compatibility across heterogeneous hosts. Migration requires verification of a common CPU baseline, machine type, QEMU/libvirt versions, firmware, and device support.

Selection strategy: Choose host-passthrough for a single host without migration, host-model for a cluster with the same architecture, and custom plus a vendor model for a heterogeneous cluster. NixOS users use host-passthrough by default.

cache controls page-cache and write-acknowledgment semantics; io selects the I/O backend. Performance and consistency after power loss also depend on guest flushes, the host filesystem, and storage. unsafe ignores flushes and is unsuitable for workloads that require durability. Verify a block-device source using its stable /dev/disk/by-id/<DISK_ID> path and capacity; selecting the wrong device directly affects a real disk.
I/O mode; choose native for raw block devices
Recommendation: Use virtio for all Linux VMs, with <model type='virtio'/>. Use virtio for Windows VMs too after installing virtio-win drivers.
Always use virsh edit <domain> rather than editing files directly. virsh edit validates the XML on exit and refuses to save malformed XML.
Export inactive XML before editing a persistent definition; there is no need to destroy/undefine it first:
define updates the persistent definition; a running instance does not automatically receive every change. Choose live/config hotplug operations separately, or schedule a normal restart.
No restart needed after some changes: Certain devices, such as disks and network adapters, support hotplugging. Apply these changes to a running VM with virsh attach-device / virsh detach-device.

The following demonstrates only an offline backup of file-based disks. Shut the VM down normally first and confirm that all writers have stopped. Internal snapshots, or “taking a snapshot first,” do not automatically make an ordinary cp of a changing disk consistent. For online backups, use libvirt backup/block jobs and verify application consistency and the complete chain.

convert flattens the selected chain into a standalone image, but the XML still points to the original path. When restoring, update paths in a copy of the XML and check UUIDs, MAC addresses, and permissions. Separately back up UEFI NVRAM, software TPM state, secure recovery material corresponding to libvirt secrets references, and disk-encryption recovery keys. Do not put real keys in public XML or logs. Backends such as block devices, RBD, and LVM need their corresponding consistent-backup workflows. Test restored copies on an isolated network to avoid identity conflicts with the original VM.

--os-variant is not decorative: it affects defaults such as the disk bus, network-adapter model, and USB controller. An exact match is recommended.

Before cloning, confirm that the source VM is stopped, the destination file does not exist, and enough space is available. --auto-clone can select names/storage automatically, or you can specify --file explicitly as in this example; do not mix these two approaches. A clone needs changes to guest identities such as hostname, networking, machine-id, and SSH host keys. Use virt-sysprep only on an offline copy. UEFI/TPM state and passthrough devices require separate handling.
Shutdown: Start with shutdown and check domstate; after a timeout, use the application's recovery plan to decide whether to force power-off
Editing: Always use virsh edit; do not edit files directly
Backups: Persistent XML + complete, consistent disks + external state such as NVRAM/TPM, with a verified restore
Snapshots: Choose internal/external according to backend support and recovery goals; verify the complete chain. Snapshots do not replace backups
Monitoring: Use virt-top for a live view, domstats for collection, and event for alerts
